svg.title: SGD update and the learning-rate trade-off
svg.desc: A hand-drawn figure in two parts. The upper card gives the update rule, theta new equals theta old minus alpha times the gradient, applied to every weight and bias once per step, beside the two lines of code that implement it and a note that the whole optimiser holds one number and no state. Below, three loss-curve panels on one shared vertical scale. Too small, in warn tan, shows a nearly flat line: steps are taken and none of them get anywhere. Right-sized, in success green at alpha equals one, shows a smooth descent still falling at ten thousand epochs. Too large, in alert red, shows a curve oscillating with growing amplitude as each step overshoots the minimum. A note records that the panels share one scale so the diverging run is drawn as large as it actually is. A band states that large steps explore and small steps converge, that one constant cannot do both across a whole run, and that every optimiser in Parts 23 to 27 is a way of not having to choose.
svg.text: Vanilla SGD, and its one knob
Subtract a scaled gradient from every parameter. The scale is the only thing there is to choose.
applied to every weight and every bias, once per step
The whole optimiser. It holds one number and no state.
The loss barely moves. Steps are
taken; none of them get anywhere.
every time, and the loss grows.
All three panels share one vertical scale, so the diverging run is drawn as large as it actually is.
Large steps explore and small steps converge, and one constant cannot do both jobs across a whole training run.
Every optimiser in Parts 23 to 27 is a way of not having to choose one number and live with it.
